taxonomic_note: Accepted as Euphorbia villifera Scheele by current Kew/POWO and Flora of North America. Chamaesyce villifera is the principal legacy name in this project; Chamaesyce stanfieldii/Euphorbia stanfieldii are also treated as synonyms.
look_here_first: LOOK AT GROWTH HABIT + THE NODES, NOT JUST THE COMMON NAME. Euphorbia villifera generally has ascending/upright branches rather than a flat, rooted mat. At opposite-leaf nodes, its stipules are DISTINCT, THREADLIKE (filiform), unlike E. serpens' fused broad triangular scales. Leaf/stem surfaces are PAPILLATE under strong magnification; most specimens are LONG-HAIRED but completely glabrous forms occur. Most useful reproductive confirmation: SMOOTH THREE-LOBED capsule whose cocci may be elongated into an internally EMPTY tip, which needs DISSECTION to prove. Current public photos show hair, a leaf node, developing capsule and styles but do NOT prove the exact stipule identity, cellular papillae, dissected empty tip or mature seed sculpture. Hays inclusion remains PROVISIONAL and native metrics excluded.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays-local legacy Chamaesyce source; current Kew explicitly treats Chamaesyce villifera as a synonym of accepted Euphorbia villifera, native in Texas.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Installed for active visual learning; broader exact-county reconciliation deferred.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Euphorbiaceae; Euphorbia section Anisophyllum (legacy Chamaesyce). Opposite asymmetric leaves, tiny cyathia rather than normal flowers, and dry 3-lobed capsules.
morphology_keys.growth_form: Annual or perennial herb with slender taproot or sometimes thickened woody rootstock; stems usually erect to ascending, rarely prostrate/decumbent, about 10–30 cm.
morphology_keys.stems: Papillate; usually villous but sometimes glabrous. Hair presence alone is therefore not absolute.
morphology_keys.leaves: Opposite; blades ovate, about 3–12 × 2–10 mm, base asymmetric and rounded to slightly cordate, margins entire or serrulate, surfaces usually villous but sometimes glabrous; leaf surfaces are papillate.
morphology_keys.stipules: Distinct, filiform, usually undivided, rarely split into 2–3 segments, about 0.3–0.7 mm; this differs strongly from the fused deltate stipule scale of E. serpens.
morphology_keys.cyathium: Cyathia solitary at distal nodes; 4 pink glands, oval/oblong/trapezoidal, with white-to-pink appendages.
morphology_keys.fruit: Capsule oblate-deltoid, about 1.5–2 × 2.1–3.1 mm, glabrous; cocci are often elongated and terminate in an empty distal portion.
morphology_keys.seed: Seeds gray-brown to red-brown, ovoid-oblong, weakly 4-angled, about 1–1.4 × 0.6–0.8 mm; smooth, faintly rugose, or with inconspicuous transverse ridges.
best_field_traits: Usually upright/ascending branches, about 10–30 cm tall; rare prostrate plants possible. Distinctive relative to typical prostrate sandmat trio but not alone decisive.
Opposite ovate leaves about 3–12 mm long with asymmetric base, sometimes soft-hairy and sometimes essentially glabrous.
Stipules distinctly separate, narrow, FILIFORM and small (about 0.3–0.7 mm): inspect with loupe at BOTH sides of leaf node; existing closeup doesn't independently resolve them from hairs.
Leaf blades and stems PAPILLATE under magnification. Surface texture in photos is NOT proof of individual papillae.
Long soft VILLOUS hairs frequently present on foliage and stems but some forms can be glabrous; don't decide from hair density alone.
Small pink cyathial glands with white-pink appendages; capsule smooth/glabrous and approximately 1.5–2 by 2.1–3.1 mm.
Capsule lobes (cocci) may have elongated external ends enclosing an EMPTY DISTAL PORTION, needing sectioned/dissected fruit to verify.
Seeds about 1–1.4 mm, weakly four-angled, smooth/faintly rugose or weakly transversely ridged; never substitute the mixed seeds-on-palm photo as diagnostic seed evidence.
FNA places species in Texas Edwards Plateau and westward Trans-Pecos. Project Hays county target check still PROVISIONAL; not converted automatically to confirmed metrics.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Against E. serpens: villifera is usually erect/ascending, has distinct filiform stipules and papillate surfaces; serpens is a glabrous prostrate mat that roots at nodes and has fused deltate stipule scales. Against E. prostrata: villifera has filiform stipules and glabrous capsules with often empty-tipped elongated cocci; prostrata does not root at nodes, has upper-free/lower-fused stipules, and has crisped-villous capsule keels.
field_photo_steps: 1. Photograph the ENTIRE plant showing upright/ascending habit with ground and ruler.
2. Photograph a complete pair of opposite mature leaves plus node with 1 mm scale.
3. Under 10×–20×, isolate at least TWO true separate threadlike stipules from hair strands at the node; photograph attachment.
4. Under strong side lighting, get a leaf-surface macro resolving individual papillate bumps versus long soft hairs.
5. Photograph intact GLABROUS three-lobed capsule and styles with 1 mm scale; do not call the empty distal tip proven.
6. If permitted, dissect an old mature capsule under loupe to show elongated lobe tip with empty inside, THEN photograph a true released seed.
7. Compare with E. serpens (fused broad stipule, smooth glabrous mat), E. prostrata (hairy capsule keels, strong seed ridges), E. maculata (hairs on fruit faces, shallow seed furrows).
morphology_keys.crew_script: See how this spurge often grows UP and has leaf pairs? Now zoom into the node: villifera should have separate tiny THREADLIKE stipules, not a single fused triangular scale. Check the fruit: it should be smooth; in mature dissected capsules the lobes can extend past the seed cavity. Notice how hairy the leaves may be—but don't bet the ID on fuzz alone, because it can also grow smooth.
morphology_keys.caution: Euphorbia latex may irritate eyes/skin. Avoid breaking stems unnecessarily; fruit dissection only when a loose mature sample and safety protocols permit.

comparisons.key_distinctions: The combination is important: usually ascending/erect habit + distinctly separate filiform stipules + papillate blade surface + GLABROUS capsule with often elongated internally EMPTY distal coccus tips. Prostrata's capsule keels are HAIRY, maculata has hairs across fruit FACES; serpens fruit is also glabrous, so separate from serpens by fused broad stipules, rooting mat habit, and papillate villifera surfaces. Some villifera individuals are glabrous; never use leaf fuzz alone.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Villifera: find the NODE and check the GLABROUS capsule
steps: Find a hairy leaf and smooth-looking rounded fruit; remember hair density ALONE is unreliable.
Look at the red stem NODE where opposite leaves meet and a green capsule with projecting styles occurs.
Use the microscope or hand lens to resolve TWO distinct THREADLIKE stipules (this is still a missing photograph).
Inspect papillate leaf texture and dissected elongated empty distal capsule tip where available; otherwise preserve uncertain identification.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Usually ascending + separate threadlike stipules + papillate blades + glabrous capsule with prolonged empty-tipped cocci = E. villifera. Photos currently prove only coarser supportive structures.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Do not confuse pink/white styles with threadlike stipules or leaf hairs with stipules. Do not label unverified tiny surface texture as papillae, external pointed lobes as internally hollow, or loose mixed material as identified mature seeds. Photo count does not equal proof.
training_gallery_order: 08: Find opposite leaf junction, developing capsule and styles (3 verified arrows)

06: Loose pieces on palm are NOT proven seeds; do not use for mature seed ID
